q: Which dispatcher would you use for a blocking database read, parsing a large JSON file, and updating the UI? How does withContext fit in?
a: Dispatchers.IO for blocking I/O such as a file or blocking database read, Dispatchers.Default for CPU-heavy work such as parsing or sorting, and Dispatchers.Main for UI. withContext switches the current coroutine to another dispatcher for a block, suspends until it finishes and returns its result, so a suspend function can make itself safe to call from the main thread.
explanation: IO has a larger thread pool because its threads spend most of their time waiting; Default is sized to CPU cores. Main-safe functions own their dispatcher switch, so callers do not need to know. Libraries such as Room and Retrofit already provide main-safe suspend functions, so wrapping them again is unnecessary.
mistake: Running CPU-heavy parsing on Dispatchers.IO, or wrapping already main-safe library calls in withContext.
rubric: Matches IO, Default and Main to the right work
Explains what withContext does and returns
Describes main-safe functions
Knows library suspend functions may already be main-safe

q: Does declaring a property with val make the object it refers to immutable?
a: No. val means the reference cannot be reassigned, while var can be. The object may still be mutable: a val of type MutableList can still be changed, and a val with a custom getter can return a different value on each read. Real immutability comes from read-only types holding immutable data, such as data classes with only val properties.
explanation: Prefer val by default because it removes one source of change. Exposing a read-only List type over a mutable list still lets the owner change it underneath callers, so copy or use immutable collections when that matters.
mistake: Assuming a val collection or object can never change.
rubric: Distinguishes reference reassignment from object mutation
Gives a mutable-object example
Mentions custom getters
Explains how to achieve real immutability

q: How do launch and async differ, including how they report failures?
a: launch starts work that returns no result and gives you a Job; async returns a Deferred whose value you read with await(). With structured concurrency, a failure in either cancels the parent scope unless it is supervised. async also rethrows the exception from await(), and under a SupervisorJob a failed async that nobody awaits can go unnoticed.
explanation: Use async only for concurrent results you will await, typically inside coroutineScope so all children finish or fail together. A CoroutineExceptionHandler applies to launch-based root coroutines, not to async, whose errors surface at await().
mistake: Using async for fire-and-forget work and never calling await, which hides failures.
rubric: Explains Job versus Deferred
Describes failure propagation to the parent
Notes that await rethrows

q: What is a companion object, and how does it differ from Java static members?
a: A companion object is a singleton object declared inside a class; you call its members through the class name. Unlike static members it is a real object: it can implement interfaces, be passed around, and have extensions. Use it for factory functions and constants, adding @JvmStatic or @JvmField only when Java callers need true statics.
explanation: Because it is an object, a companion can satisfy an interface such as a factory contract. Top-level functions and properties are often simpler when nothing ties them to the class. const val is for compile-time primitives and strings.
mistake: Moving every helper into a companion object out of Java habit when a top-level function would do.

q: Why can a program start 100,000 coroutines but not 100,000 threads?
a: Coroutines are lightweight: a suspended coroutine is a small object storing where to resume, not an operating-system thread with its own stack. Many coroutines share a small pool of dispatcher threads and release the thread whenever they suspend. Blocking calls still hold the underlying thread, so they must run on a suitable dispatcher.
explanation: The compiler turns suspend functions into state machines with continuations, so waiting costs memory for that state rather than a parked thread. The benefit disappears if code blocks inside a coroutine, because then each one does occupy a thread.
mistake: Assuming coroutines make blocking code non-blocking or run in parallel automatically.
rubric: Explains suspension instead of blocking
Contrasts coroutine memory with thread stacks
Mentions sharing a dispatcher thread pool
Warns about blocking calls
followups: What happens if 1,000 coroutines call Thread.sleep on Dispatchers.Default?
